answers.text: Say the delivery date changes and a pallet or two gets added — I'd want three lines in a fixed order: delivery date, item and quantity, then what's changed, nothing extra. That keeps the same email giving the same three lines every time.

For a week's claims, fixed fields in order — date, amount, category, submitter — then total the amount column, no hand adjustment. If two claims look like duplicates, same date, amount, person, list them separately and flag them rather than merging. Two different people running it on the same claims should land on the same structure and total.

The price maths is right, so that's not the issue. The real problem's the dates — the call was the 14th, the new delivery date's the 19th, but the email also says that's three days out from today. Five days isn't three days, so those two don't line up.

62 up from 54 is about 15%, that bit's fine. But 3 late out of 62 isn't 97%, more like 95%, so that on-time number's wrong. I didn't look closely at the stock figures, 170 plus 170 does equal 340 so I let that one go.

I'd go with Output 2 since it shows the actual numbers, 612,000 and 25,100, and how they get to 4.1%. Output 1 just states the percentage with nothing behind it, so you can't tell where that number came from.

I'd send Reply 2, it has the order reference and the credit reference in it so someone can look them up later if needed. Reply 1 isn't necessarily wrong, it's just that the '10% credit' in it can't be checked against anything as written. I wouldn't scrap it though, I'd just get the reference numbers added before it goes out.
1. Address — no. 2. Total sales figure — yes. 3. Pricing plan — no. 4. Spec sheet — yes. 5. Mobile number — no. Kept these short since I was fairly confident on all of them.

The pricing and discount figures I'd keep out of an unvetted tool, that's commercially sensitive. Same with the confidentiality clause, since it names both companies directly, I'd be careful with that part too.
Before it goes to my manager, I check the delivery numbers in the report against the warehouse log myself. I do that right after the draft's done, before it's sent up.

Step 1 matters — if the order details get read wrong at the start, everything after's built on that. But the real gate should be at step 4, right before the confirmation goes out automatically, since once it's sent the customer has that delivery date in writing. The gate should check the extracted items and quantities against the original email, and that stock isn't just barely enough to cover it.
